lesson_title: The Messy Lab That Saved Millions
hook_text: In 1928 a scientist came back from holiday to a dish of mould he should have thrown away. It became the most important medicine of the century.
clip_script: London, 1928. Alexander Fleming comes back from holiday to a messy lab. One dish of bacteria has a blob of blue-green mould on it, and all around the mould there is a clear ring where the bacteria have died. The mould is Penicillium, and the substance it makes is penicillin, the first antibiotic. It breaks the walls of bacteria so they burst, and before it existed an infected cut could kill you. But microbes were helping us long before that. Bacteria turn the sugar in milk into acid, and that is how yoghurt and amasi get thick and sour. Yeast, a fungus, breathes out carbon dioxide in dough, and that is why bread rises. And every dead leaf in every forest is broken down by bacteria and fungi into minerals that feed the next plant. Most microbes are not germs. They are the clean-up crew, the cooks and the doctors.
visual_style: A whiteboard petri dish with a mould blob and a clear ring; then quick icons for a yoghurt bowl, a rising loaf with bubbles and a leaf crumbling into soil.
pacing: Story-led opening, then a quick three-part montage, ending on a confident line.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and give every useful microbe its job.
